approved: National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Mandatory Credit Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2019
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill would make it compulsory for large banks to share details of their customers' credit accounts with credit reporting agencies.
The bill would also let lenders report when a borrower gets a hardship arrangement, such as a payment deferral, on their credit file.
The mandatory regime would apply from 1 April 2020 to large authorised deposit-taking institutions, which accounted for over 80 per cent of household lending in June 2019.
Requires large authorised deposit-taking institutions to supply credit information on consumer accounts to credit reporting bodies.
Creates a new type of credit information called financial hardship information that can be reported when a consumer's payment is altered by a permanent variation or a hardship arrangement.
Allows credit reporting bodies to share the mandated information only under conditions set out in regulations.
Large authorised deposit-taking institutions, credit reporting bodies, and consumers with credit accounts or hardship arrangements.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2021-02-03.43.1) to the usual [second reading motion](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/), which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill). ### Amendment text > *At the end of the motion, add: ", but the Senate:* > > *(a) notes that:* > >> *(i) when introducing this bill on 5 December 2019, the Treasurer, the Hon Josh Frydenberg MP, said in his second reading speech that with this legislation "credit providers will have a more complete picture of a consumer's financial situation [which] will help them to better price credit and meet their responsible lending obligations",* >> >> *(ii) with its National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Supporting Economic Recovery) Bill 2020, the Government is seeking to repeal legislated responsible lending obligations from the National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009 (the NCCP Act), and* >> >> *(iii) in the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry report, which was released on 1 February 2019, Recommendation 1 stated that "the NCCP Act should not be amended to alter the obligation to assess unsuitability", which was accepted by the Government; and* > > *(b) calls on the Government to honour its acceptance of Recommendation 1 of the Royal Commission and withdraw its National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Supporting Economic Recovery) Bill 2020".*

The speaker supported the National Consumer Credit Protection Amendment (Mandatory Credit Reporting and Other Measures) Bill 2019 but announced Labor would move amendments to allow consumers free access to their credit information every 10 days, require disclosure of credit scores, and address hardship flags that unfairly affect credit scores during natural disasters.

The bill mandates the five largest banks to supply 50% of comprehensive credit information to credit-reporting bodies by 1 April 2020 and the remaining accounts by 1 April 2021, introduces financial hardship reporting protections, and requires an independent review by 1 October 2023.

The bill mandates major banks to supply detailed credit information to credit reporting agencies from 1 April 2020 and introduces two hardship flags for individuals experiencing financial hardship. Labor supported the bill as a codification of current industry practice with improved consumer protections and data security measures.

The government's mandatory comprehensive credit-reporting regime, applying from 1 April 2020, will require Australia's largest banks (with assets over $100 billion) to supply full credit data to reporting bodies, increasing competition and consumer access to credit while strengthening privacy protections and prohibiting the use of financial hardship information as the sole reason for freezing accounts or reducing credit limits.

Centre Alliance supported the bill but moved an amendment arguing that retaining hardship information on credit reports for 12 months is unfair, may drive people to high-cost payday loans, and that the government has failed to introduce legislation addressing the independent Review of Small Amount Credit Contracts for over 1,000 days.
